topics: 🔔 A Silent Bell Stays Impure — Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Ḥanina and Rabbi Yoḥanan's two reasons
🥾 The Metal Animal-Shoe — must a new use for a person resemble the vessel's original use?
👑 City of Gold — Rabbi Meir, the Rabbis, and Rabbi Eliezer on the Jerusalem-of-gold tiara
🎀 Kelila and Kamra — which tiaras and belts a woman may wear into the public domain
💍 A Ring's Status — with an engraved seal it's a burden, without one it's an ornament

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Reused Vessels, Gold Tiaras, and a Woman's Ring
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 59a–59b
overview.hebrewSource: לֹא תֵּצֵא אִשָּׁה בְּעִיר שֶׁל זָהָב, וְאִם יָצְתָה חַיֶּיבֶת חַטָּאת
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens by resolving the previous amud's question — why a bell whose clapper was removed keeps its earlier ritual impurity — by weighing whether its reuse (for sound versus for water) must resemble its original function, a principle then tested on a metal animal-shoe repurposed by a fleeing soldier. The mishna's discussion then turns to what a woman may wear into the public domain on Shabbat: an 'ir shel zahav', a gold ornament engraved with the image of Jerusalem like the one Rabbi Akiva made his wife, and whether it is a forbidden burden or a permitted ornament. The Gemara works through parallel disputes about the kelila (a tiara) and the kamra (a belt), and closes by asking why a ring with an engraved seal is a burden for a woman while a plain ring is an ornament.

slides.title: 🔔 Why a Silent Bell Stays Impure
slides.subtitle: Two amoraim, two reasons — and a swap to resolve a contradiction

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: A bell whose clapper was removed still carries its earlier impurity. It was stated: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Ḥanina and Rabbi Yoḥanan each gave a reason.

lines.speaker: Reason A
lines.text: Since it is still fit to be struck against earthenware, producing a similar sound

lines.speaker: Reason B
lines.text: Since it is still fit to give a child water to drink

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: But we know from elsewhere — the case of a metal animal-shoe — that Rabbi Yoḥanan requires a new use to resemble the vessel's original use (מֵעֵין מְלָאכָה רִאשׁוֹנָה). Giving a child water has nothing to do with ringing!

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: So reverse the attributions: it was Rabbi Yoḥanan who said 'fit to strike on earthenware' — sound-producing, matching the bell's original use — and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Ḥanina who permitted the unrelated water-use.

callout.label: Why swap here and not elsewhere:
callout.text: The sandal-of-an-animal case (next slide) independently proves Rabbi Yoḥanan requires a same-type reuse — so this is the dispute that must be corrected.

slides.title: 🥾 The Metal Animal-Shoe — Fit for a Person How?
slides.subtitle: A shoe an animal can no longer use remains impure only if a person can reuse it
rows: Drinking water from it during a war
If the shoe is dirty and repulsive, no one would drink from it — it becomes pure
Smearing oil on the body during a war
Stays impure even if dirty — one still uses a grimy vessel to smear oil
Strapping it to his own foot while fleeing battle, to run over thorns
If the shoe is too heavy to wear, it becomes pure, though it would still hold oil

callout.label: The point:
callout.text: Only Rabbi Yoḥanan's answer keeps the SAME kind of use — footwear. That is the proof that he alone requires the new use to resemble the original one.

slides.title: 👑 City of Gold — Ornament or Burden?
slides.subtitle: A gold tiara engraved with Jerusalem, 'like the one Rabbi Akiva made for his wife'

boxes.title: Rabbi Meir
items: It is a burden, not an ornament
Going out with it makes one liable to a sin-offering

boxes.title: The Rabbis
items: It IS an ornament — no sin-offering if she goes out
Still forbidden ab initio: she might remove it to show a friend and come to carry it

boxes.title: Rabbi Eliezer
items: Only an important woman wears a city of gold, and an important woman does not remove her ornaments to show them off

slides.title: 🎀 Kelila and Kamra — One Ruling, Two Towns Respond
slides.subtitle: A tiara and a belt, argued twice over and then put into practice

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rav forbids going out with a kelila (a tiara-like ornament); Shmuel permits it
2️⃣ First version: all agree a fully metal kelila is forbidden; they disagree only about one woven with metal — Rav treats the metal as primary (forbidden), Shmuel the fabric (permitted)

3️⃣ Rav Ashi reverses it: all agree a purely woven kelila is permitted; they disagree only about a metal one — fear she'll remove and carry it (Rav) vs. only an 'important woman' wears one and won't (Shmuel)
4️⃣ When Levi taught 'the kelila is permitted' in Neharde'a, 24 women went out wearing one; when Rabba bar Avuh taught the same in Meḥoza, 18 went out from a single alleyway
5️⃣ Related: a gilded kamra (belt) is permitted, like a king's belt; but two belts worn together are not — one becomes a mere burden; a short cloak needs straps or it is forbidden

slides.title: 💍 A Ring's Status — Sealed vs. Plain
slides.subtitle: The same mishna's ring-rule seems to contradict a mishna in Kelim
rows: An ornament — forbidden to go out with it, but exempt if she does
Impure — counted as a woman's ornament
A burden — liable to a sin-offering if she goes out with it
Impure — no distinction made from a plain ring

callout.label: Rabbi Zeira resolves it:
callout.text: Our mishna follows Rabbi Neḥemya, who says 'for a ring, follow its seal' (and for a yoke, 'follow its rods') — a sealed ring is a man's tool, so for a woman it is a burden. The Kelim mishna follows the Rabbis, who look only at the ring's own primary material.

summary.principle: A vessel keeps its former status only if reused in a way that resembles its original function, and an item worn by a woman counts as an ornament — permitted, or at least not liable — only when its normal purpose and its wearer's habits make it unlikely she would remove and carry it.

flowSteps.content: 🔔 A clapperless bell stays impure only via a REUSE matching its original purpose (Rabbi Yoḥanan)
🥾 Proven from the animal-shoe: only 'strapped to a fleeing soldier's foot' preserves that same-type use

columns.content: 👑 City of gold: burden (R' Meir) vs. ornament people still might remove (Rabbis) vs. safe on an important woman (R' Eliezer)
💍 Sealed ring = a burden (a man's tool); plain ring = a true ornament

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: whether an item may leave the house on Shabbat turns on its real function and on whether its wearer is likely to slip it off

quiz.q: In the Gemara's resolved version, why does Rabbi Yoḥanan say a clapperless bell keeps its ritual impurity?
o: Because it is still fit to give a child water to drink
Because it is still fit to be struck against earthenware, producing a similar sound
Because metal never loses impurity
Because a craftsman could repair it
quiz.e: After the Gemara reverses the attribution, Rabbi Yoḥanan is the one who requires a same-type reuse, and striking the bell on earthenware still produces sound — matching its original purpose.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yoḥanan, how does a metal animal-shoe get reused by a PERSON in a way that keeps it susceptible to impurity?
o: It is melted down into jewelry
It is used to smear oil on the body
It is strapped to one's own foot while fleeing battle, to run over thorns
It is used as a drinking cup
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan's answer preserves the same type of use as the original (footwear), which is why the Gemara uses this source to prove he requires a same-type reuse.

quiz.q: What is an 'ir shel zahav' (city of gold), as the Gemara describes it?
o: A miniature siege engine
A gold tiara engraved with a depiction of Jerusalem, like the one Rabbi Akiva made for his wife
A type of ancient coin
A woven belt
quiz.e: Rabba bar bar Ḥana said in Rabbi Yoḥanan's name that it is 'Jerusalem of Gold,' the ornament Rabbi Akiva made for his wife.

quiz.q: Why do the Rabbis forbid going out with a city-of-gold ornament ab initio, even though they consider it an ornament and not a burden?
o: Because it is too heavy to wear comfortably
Because they fear she might remove it to show a friend and come to carry it in the public domain
Because gold ornaments cannot become ritually impure
Because only priests' wives may wear it
quiz.e: The Rabbis agree it is an ornament (so one who goes out with it is exempt from a sin-offering), but still forbid it ab initio out of concern she will take it off to show someone and end up carrying it.

quiz.q: Why does the mishna treat a ring with an engraved seal as a burden for a woman, unlike a plain ring?
o: A sealed ring is a man's tool for sealing documents, so it is not a woman's ornament
Sealed rings are always more valuable and thus forbidden
Sealed rings cannot become ritually impure
Sealed rings are permitted only for brides
quiz.e: Following Rabbi Neḥemya's principle that a ring's status follows its seal, a ring bearing a seal used for sealing documents is treated as a man's implement — a burden, not an ornament, for a woman.
